episode_thesis: Rob Carver answers listener questions with one recurring logic: use only as much leverage, complexity and cost as the expected performance justifies (volatility-scaled sizing, Sharpe over skew, simple signals, test what you trade, markets before more trend variants). He then reads a minutes-to-centuries paper as showing momentum from about an hour to a year and mean reversion outside that range. In mid-February 2025 he argues Trump's tariffs, deportations and institutional instability are inflationary and raise the equity risk premium, which should show first in bonds and gold and favours price-following CTAs, while host Niels Kaastrup-Larsen adds an erosion-of-trust and Fourth Turning view and a critique of multi-strategy pass-through fees.

speakers.name: Rob Carver
speakers.role: systematic futures trader and author (ex-AHL), answering listener questions
speakers.speaker_note: Main speaker. In C23 the turn in which he agrees that a price-based strategy is good appears to start mid-paragraph after Niels' trust-erosion point (ledger correction: probable Rob). C12-1 (35-40% of research budget on execution) is Niels' recollection, not Rob's.

worldview_premises.premise: A futures price equals spot plus yield minus funding; for a yieldless asset like gold the premium over spot is essentially the borrowing cost, so carry is observable in the futures-spot gap.
worldview_premises.support: pricing identity plus the current gold example

worldview_premises.premise: Appropriate leverage is set by the Kelly criterion, i.e. by expected performance. Risk above roughly 20-30% volatility is probably more than any plausible expected return justifies.
worldview_premises.support: rule of thumb, applied to 2x S&P (30-40% vol) vs 1.5x 60/40 (about 12-15% vol) without checking product documents

worldview_premises.premise: Leveraged ETFs on volatile underlyings drift toward zero over long holds because of volatility drag.
worldview_premises.support: arithmetic example (down 10% then up 10% ends below the start; worse with leverage)

worldview_premises.premise: For a trader who can lever freely, volatility has effectively no price, so Sharpe is the right comparison metric. Leverage cannot create skew, so skew is the only thing leverage cannot buy.
worldview_premises.support: first principles

worldview_premises.premise: Terminal wealth (geometric mean / CAGR) is the key metric, and the Sharpe ratio one should give up to buy positive skew is small, so the higher-Sharpe strategy is usually better.
worldview_premises.support: his own simulation of terminal wealth over Sharpe and skew combinations (blog post)

worldview_premises.premise: Diversification comes from low correlation: a new market correlates about 0.4-0.5 with existing ones, a new trend system about 0.8-0.9, and a different style such as carry about 0.5 once many markets are held.
worldview_premises.support: experience with his own system, rough figures

worldview_premises.premise: Momentum works across futures from roughly an hour up to about a year (plus, he suggests, perhaps 18 months); mean reversion dominates below an hour and beyond a year.
worldview_premises.support: Safari and Schmidhuber paper (cubic polynomial fit across horizons, data back to 1692) and his own earlier book

worldview_premises.premise: Mean reversion at very short horizons exists because high-frequency traders buy the bid and sell the ask around a bouncing price.
worldview_premises.support: market-structure argument

worldview_premises.premise: Every indicator lags because it uses the past. A moving average or EMA is just a weighting function over past returns, and nonlinear tweaks add parameters and overfitting risk.
worldview_premises.support: first principles; his own test of a short-horizon mean-reversion add-on

worldview_premises.premise: Prefer the simplest version of a strategy and do not add many signals for tiny marginal gains.
worldview_premises.support: Occam's razor; complexity cost

worldview_premises.premise: Machine learning and neural nets on existing data are low-yield research (Renaissance excepted). The bigger research payoffs are new markets, execution at scale and alternative data.
worldview_premises.support: his AHL experience and impression of where firms invest; no data given

worldview_premises.premise: ETF wrappers usually cost more than direct futures (fees, provider profit, slippage from size), and liquidity varies, so test with the instrument you will trade.
worldview_premises.support: cost decomposition argument

worldview_premises.premise: Multi-strategy pod fees are opaque because expenses are charged to the client account outside the headline fees, and winning managers get paid even when the whole fund loses.
worldview_premises.support: industry knowledge; contrast with UCITS cost transparency

worldview_premises.premise: He is a poor discretionary trader (good entry, no exit rule), while a systematic trader can attribute every trade exactly. Short windows of performance are noise.
worldview_premises.support: his own bond trade and the 1% year-to-date result after seven weeks

worldview_premises.premise: Unstable regulation, rule of law and frequently changed tariffs raise the risk premium, and a higher risk premium is bad for equities.
worldview_premises.support: economic reasoning (businesses want certainty more than lower regulation); no data

worldview_premises.premise: Bond investors are more professional and conservative than (increasingly retail) equity investors, so credit and bond markets tend to flag trouble before equities.
worldview_premises.support: 2007-08 anecdote; he is reluctant to say one market always leads another

mechanism_chains.topic: Position sizing: fixed contracts vs volatility scaling, Sharpe vs skew

steps.to: explosive moves (cocoa 2024) hit an unscaled position, creating positive outliers; losers are closed so no matching negative tail
steps.why: position is not cut when volatility rises

steps.to: highest Sharpe ratio, less positive skew
steps.why: reduces contracts when volatility or price rises

steps.to: terminal-wealth simulation says higher Sharpe more than compensates for lost upside volatility, so choose volatility scaling
steps.why: volatility only matters through terminal wealth; benefit of positive skew is limited

mechanism_chains.evidence: Quantica Q4 2024 paper and his own simulation (blog post); both find the lower Sharpe of fixed sizing is not paid for by skew.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Investors with a strong preference for positive skew may rationally give up more Sharpe. Very high Sharpe with heavy leverage or opacity can hide negative skew (Madoff).

mechanism_chains.fails_when: Costs at short horizons; long-horizon signals are hard to show significant and may show negative Sharpe in backtests.

decision_process.practice: Turn any predictor (a 'feature') into a forecast by scaling it, like a z-score. Regressing volatility-normalised returns on the signal gives the same scaling. He does not remove the intercept (systematic long or short bias).
decision_process.why: the coefficient says how big the forecast is; he prefers to keep bias

decision_process.practice: The forecasting target is risk-adjusted returns.
Fixed-risk (volatility-scaled) position sizing, preferring Sharpe and terminal wealth over skew.
decision_process.why: highest Sharpe; skew gain does not pay for lower Sharpe

decision_process.practice: Keep total risk below about 20-30% volatility. Check how correlation could change the volatility of stacked products. Be wary of high-Sharpe strategies needing leverage or opacity.
decision_process.why: Kelly: expected performance rarely justifies more

decision_process.practice: Add markets before additional trend variants. Once many markets are held, add a different style (carry). Adding systems needs no extra capital if automated.
decision_process.why: correlation 0.4-0.5 for new markets vs 0.8-0.9 for a new trend system vs about 0.5 for carry

decision_process.practice: Consider an absolute long-term mean-reversion (negative multi-year momentum) signal in addition to relative mean reversion. He has not tested it recently and notes long signals rarely reach significance.
decision_process.why: simpler than relative, probably diversifying, supported by the time-scale paper and equity literature

decision_process.practice: Reject nonlinear responses to recent observations and tiny-gain extra signals (a one-week mean-reversion add-on gave insignificant gains).
decision_process.why: added parameters, overfit risk, complexity not worth it

decision_process.practice: Backtest with the instrument you trade (test what you trade, trade what you test). Compare total returns, adding the risk-free rate to back-adjusted futures prices.
decision_process.why: ETF includes interest and costs, futures margin earns interest not shown in prices

decision_process.practice: Small traders use a simple few-line execution algorithm. Large funds trading hundreds of millions to billions need execution research. Compare own annual roll cost with the ETF's full expense ratio.
decision_process.why: execution matters more as assets grow

decision_process.practice: Handle missing data by going flat until enough prices exist to form forecasts and volatility. Never interpolate prices in a backtest, except overnight hours for volatility estimation using a Brownian bridge.
decision_process.why: interpolation is wrong 99.9% of the time

decision_process.practice: Stay systematic. Discretionary trades without predefined stops or exit criteria are avoided.
decision_process.why: his bond trade caught the yield top but was closed flat

speakers.evidence_style: Mixed. First-principles arithmetic (volatility drag, Kelly, pricing identity), his own simulations and backtests reported in blog posts, and readings of two papers (Quantica, Safari and Schmidhuber). He explicitly welcomes hard evidence over his own guesses and distrusts AI-suggested fixes, but his policy analysis is reasoned argument without data.

speakers.name: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
speakers.role: host, Top Traders Unplugged, veteran hedge fund manager
speakers.speaker_note: Mostly host questions and recaps; he states views on fees, trust erosion, risk management and the Fourth Turning. Listener questions he reads (Paul, Samuel, David and others) are not his views. The 35-40% execution budget claim is his hedged recollection of an interview, 'maybe AHL'.

worldview_premises.premise: Net-of-fee return is what matters to investors, so high fees are tolerated while net results stay good, but pass-through multi-strategy expenses make 2 and 20 look cheap.
worldview_premises.support: Bloomberg article figures (effective 7 and 20 up to 15 and 20; a fund with 15.2% gross left clients 2.8%, caption ambiguous)

worldview_premises.premise: Large institutions must be supplying the pod inflows, and it is surprising that pensions and insurers accept fees they resisted elsewhere; even UCITS expense ratios can omit costs such as research.
worldview_premises.support: his career experience of investor pushback

worldview_premises.premise: Trend followers rarely blow up unless they run highly leveraged versions, and the most room to evolve is in risk management and risk forecasting.
worldview_premises.support: industry observation; CTA index interview series

worldview_premises.premise: Few new ways of doing trend following exist, but combining more than one approach (for example moving-average crossover plus something else) may give better results.
worldview_premises.support: none beyond impression

worldview_premises.premise: Sharpe is not a great objective for trend following because it penalises upside volatility (a view he says he and many others have held).
worldview_premises.support: none given; Carver's simulation answers it

worldview_premises.premise: Decades of eroding trust in institutions cause a disconnect between value and price.
worldview_premises.support: anecdote (Oval Office image) and his previous conversations

worldview_premises.premise: Cycles between public and private trust recur, and the Fourth Turning generational cycle suggests turbulence before the period ends.
worldview_premises.support: book by Neil Howe, previous conversation; he says it is not a market forecast

speakers.evidence_style: Industry observation, index data and manager interviews, plus anecdote and cycle theory (Fourth Turning). He cites Bloomberg numbers and CTA index readings but does not test his views.

current_views.view: Early 2025 trend following was flat to mixed. Currencies were the tricky sector in February, while equities, coffee, gold and some metals contributed. Indices roughly flat (BTOP50 +1.68%, SG CTA +0.77%, SG Trend +0.57%).
Short-term traders index kept struggling, second year lagging longer-horizon trend indices; 20+ year Treasury index hurt by hot inflation data in February.
Fixed income and gold are pricing Trump-policy risk while equities show little angst.

Government bonds may turn out unsafe and equities a safe harbour in a public-private cycle turn. Conditions will become more turbulent and surprising before the period ends. He says this is not a market forecast.

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
positions.position: Net returns have been good and the money is large institutional, which surprises him given earlier fee pushback.

positions.speaker: Rob Carver

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Fee example is garbled in the caption: a 15.2% gain is said to be 'after fees' yet the client received 2.8%, so before/after is ambiguous.
The cause of the gold London-to-US movement is unknown to Rob (physical move or legal ownership; FT does not say). The explanation is partial.

Rob says Sharpe is valid only when strategies have the same skew, yet recommends maximising Sharpe across strategies with different skew. He resolves it by simulation and cites no numbers in the episode.
The Kelly rule of thumb of 20-30% volatility is given without an assumed Sharpe. The 12-15% volatility of 1.5x 60/40 is from memory, and he has not read the product documents.
The claim that ML and neural nets add little is asserted without evidence, with one exception named (Renaissance).
Extending the momentum window to about 18 months is Rob's own extrapolation from a paper that shows one year strong and two years flat, not a result of the paper.

The policy view is explicitly conditional on Trump succeeding in his plans. It is framed with a joke conclusion (buy CTAs) and is qualified by Republican pushback on tariffs, midterms, and lagged effects.
Speaker corrections applied: C12-1 is Niels' hedged recollection (maybe AHL), C12-3 and C12-4 are listener Paul's, C17-1 is Rob, C23-3 is probably Rob.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Gold futures minus spot (borrowing cost versus about 4.5-5% risk-free) as the carry input; managed-futures/equity correlation for stacked-leverage safety; US inflation prints and bond yields, which Rob expects to react first, followed by jobs data and equities with a lag; tariff announcements and Republican pushback; the midterm window of about two years. Horizons: weeks to months for the policy view, one hour to one year for momentum, beyond a year for mean reversion.
reader_inferences: (reader) Rob's theory implies a trend follower should hold the same volatility target across assets and let skew be an outcome, not a goal.
(reader) Both speakers treat bonds and gold as earlier warning markets, which suggests a testable lead-lag signal between bonds/gold and equities, though neither gives a rule.
(reader) Rob's Sharpe-over-skew argument rests on terminal wealth being the only objective; investors with drawdown or career constraints may reasonably differ.
